newsitem.title: INDIA: Merrill sees 1997 recovery for Indian stocks.
newsitem.headline: Merrill sees 1997 recovery for Indian stocks.

text.p: Bombay's benchmark stocks index is likely to touch 3800-4000 points this year, as improving fundamentals encourage foreign fund inflows, Merrill Lynch & Co and Indian affiliate DSP Financial Consultants said on Tuesday.

"We expect the combination of good performance from the agricultural sector and the lagged benefits of easier monetary policy to feed through into better overall economic performance in the second half of calendar 1997, supporting a solid recovery in earnings in 1997/98 (April-March)," Merrill said in a strategy report titled, "A Roller Coaster Ride?"
"Based on our expectations for earnings recovery we believe that the index could reach 3800-4000 during 1997 -- most probably in the second half," the report said.
Bombay's 30-share index closed 5.30 points lower at a provisional 3384.19 on Tuesday.
Merrill advised investors to pick up hotel, aluminium and oil sector stocks.
"We think it is too early to increase weightings in most commodity stocks, but the aluminium sector is an exception based on our positive view on international prices. Buy Hindalco," the report said.
Hindalco is India's largest private aluminium maker.
Merrill said hotel stocks -- which came off towards the end of last year -- were good buys in the current rally.
It advised investors to accumulate shares of oil giants Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd and Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd.
"We think there is likely to be a move towards deregulation in the oil industry in the February budget and continue to strongly emphasise the merits of the oil sector," it said.

Merrill said though a failure to address long-term issues like infrastructure bottlenecks, the fiscal deficit and the government's high debt burden could deter some investors, most concerns had been factored into equity valuations in the last two years.

The U.S. investment bank said the current rally in Indian stocks could fizzle out on a lack of strong foreign fund interest, poor results expected in 1996/97, a likely oil price hike, supply from government disinvestment and unfulfilled expectations on reforms.
"Consequently, we expect some correction before the market begins to discount the improving medium-term outlook that should emerge in the second half of 1997/98," Merrill said.
